topic_summaries.UK Drought and Water Crisis:
• BBC and multiple Evening Standard pieces focus on the immediate scale of official drought declarations, citing Environment Agency data and hosepipe bans affecting 20 million+ people
• The Guardian goes further by linking drought to broader consequences — food shortages (NFU warnings), housing target risks, and visible landscape transformation — framing it as a systemic crisis
• Channel 4 News and The Independent emphasise meteorological context (July 2026 driest in 190 years; fourth heatwave; 35C+ temperatures), while the Evening Standard also captures human relief at minor rainfall, adding a localised London angle
topic_summaries.European Wildfires and Heatwaves:
• The Guardian dominates coverage with the broadest framing — linking wildfires and heatwaves to climate science, financial stability (ECB warning), agricultural collapse, and political inaction; Channel 4 News and BBC focus more on immediate operational response and evacuation logistics
• The i and The Mirror emphasise human/consumer angles — holiday behaviour changes ("coolcations") and nuclear plant threats — while Evening Standard keeps focus local with London grass fires and drought
• GB News stands apart by covering the heatwave's novelty effects (sunken Nazi warship resurfacing) with no explicit climate crisis framing, contrasting with The Guardian and The Independent's direct attribution of events to human-caused warming
topic_summaries.Climate Politics and Corporate Accountab:
• The Guardian and Channel 4 News frame climate inaction as driven by corporate interests and political bad faith; GB News frames the same policy agenda as radical and ideologically extreme
• The Independent highlights Barclays' dual role as both climate risk analyst and fossil fuel funder; BBC and the i focus on institutional-level politics around climate declarations and green taxation
• The Guardian dominates coverage overall, emphasising accountability — from prosecuting climate crimes to Caribbean reparations — while BBC and Reform UK's South Tyneside story reflect a counter-narrative of rolling back climate commitments
topic_summaries.El Niño and Global Climate Impacts:
• The Guardian dominates coverage, framing El Niño through multiple lenses: geopolitical warnings (UN chief), ecological disruption (monsoon risk), and scientific explainers ("Godzilla" intensity)
• Daily Mail and The Independent favour dramatic, human-impact angles — lethal heat domes and shark/sea snake invasions — over policy or scientific context
• Evening Standard stands apart, focusing on long-term sea level history via a Hebridean salt marsh rather than immediate El Niño threats
topic_summaries.UK Solar and Clean Energy Transition:
• The Guardian frames solar growth positively, linking a 15-year installation high to fossil fuel costs and new pro-consumer legislation; BBC focuses on local opposition to a specific solar project, highlighting wildlife and planning concerns

• The Independent takes a consumer-advice angle on heat pumps, balancing potential benefits against practical caveats around home value and upfront costs
topic_summaries.North Sea Oil and UK Energy Policy:
• GB News dominates coverage, framing North Sea drilling as an economic and energy security imperative, amplifying Trump's pressure on Burnham and calling for immediate action; BBC and Evening Standard focus more neutrally on Burnham's "pragmatic approach" language

• The Guardian frames the story as a climate accountability issue, pressuring Burnham to honour his pledges as former mayor; GB News frames the same political moment as an opportunity to expand drilling

• BP's planned sale of its North Sea business is covered by GB News and Sky News purely as a business/energy supply story, with no environmental angle visible in the available text
topic_summaries.Suffolk Wildfire Near Sizewell Nuclear P:
• Guardian and Independent lead with emergency response details (firefighter numbers, evacuation orders); GB News emphasises authorities' reassurances that the plant is not at risk
• Daily Mail uniquely pivots to a speculative science angle — "what would happen if" a nuclear plant was hit — rather than reporting the incident directly
• Evening Standard and Channel 4 News focus on the stabilisation and scale of the blaze, with Evening Standard noting an investigation has been launched into the fire's cause

Britain could face shortages of certain foods after punishing drought in parts of England, the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) has warned as a heatwave was forecast to continue into next week.
The UK’s Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued heat health alerts for eight regions of England, with temperatures set to rise above 30C in parts of the country. UKHSA said rising temperatures may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

Farms across the country were affected by floods over the winter, making planting extremely difficult, and now in many areas they do not have access to water as irrigation is being restricted due to drought.

In some areas it has not rained for over a month, while multiple record-breaking heatwaves have hit the country since early summer, drying out the soil.

Climate breakdown is exacerbating extreme weather conditions such as droughts. This summer the Met Office has reported that England had just 8% of its average rainfall for July and it is likely to be confirmed as the driest July on record.

Two Tasmanias?

Unfortunately for hairdressers, “How’s your summer going?” is a loaded question this year. Even basking lizards and barbecue obsessives are wavering in their sun worship as cataclysmic wildfires engulf our nearest neighbours (and threaten the UK), Wales and parts of England experience drought, and farmers issue dire warnings about our food supply in the near future. Rescue centres are filling up with dehydrated hedgehogs and the Environment Agency is having to rescue fish. Lazy, joyful, sunscreen-scented days are giving way to stifling, existentially terrifying ones spent skulking in the dark (assuming you don’t need to be out in the extreme heat, as many workers do), sweatily scrolling through apocalyptic images.
Vanity Fair has decreed it’s a “sad-girl summer”, highlighting the female singer-songwriters soundtracking the myriad anxieties of an “undeniably cruel” 2026 season, but it’s not just the girlies who are sad – many of us are struggling and we still have August to survive. How?

I’m a veteran of sad-girl summers (possibly Sad summers – some people get seasonal affective disorder when it’s hot and bright). For years, July and August have sent me into an anxious, distressed funk, afflicted by brain shutdowns that leave me useless for days at a time. That means I’m ahead of the curve in finding little survival tactics, so here are some, if you find yourself struggling with what used to be the carefree, fun season.
Treat yourself like a beloved dog
Look at canine heatwave advice and apply it to yourself. Little walks in the coolest parts of the day, frozen treats, wet towels and top-ups of chilled water will all help maintain your mental equilibrium. Naps won’t hurt either.
Start your day with a book

Immerse yourself in something – anything – engaging offline for a while. Take up a temporary hobby
Distract yourself with something ultra-low stakes. Last year, I tried growing melons. My misshapen babies were inedibly disgusting, but tending them helped during my twitchiest hours. Relentless UK heatwaves turn ‘green and pleasant land’ brown


Visible impact of warming climate is impossible to ignore across landscapes that have been starved of rainfall




Half of England and the whole of Wales are officially in drought and July is set to be the driest month on record as extreme heat intensified by the climate crisis continues to grip the UK and Europe this summer.
The announcements this week by England’s Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales mark the third such event over the past five years, and come in the wake of four record-breaking heatwaves since May which have fuelled huge wildfires and left farmers, wildlife and protected habitats running out of water.



View image in fullscreen
A two-arched stone bridge thought to date to 1800 at the Llwyn-onn reservoir in the Taf Fawr valley in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales was exposed by low water levels last week. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images
England had just 7% of the long-term average rainfall for July and southern England just 1%, damaging greenery in parks, protected land and sports fields. The dry spell has also led to shrinking rivers and lakes: the Thames at Reading has recorded its lowest ever level.


Water companies are not currently expecting a threat to drinking water supplies, as record winter rainfall means reservoirs are still close to expected levels, but approximately 23 million people across England and Wales are under a hosepipe ban.
The visible impact is impossible to ignore: vast swathes of William Blake’s “green and pleasant land” are now brown and dry. The Met Office predicts that the climate crisis will make UK summers 1C-6C (1.8F-10.8F) hotter and up to 60% drier by 2070, compared with 1990.


View image in fullscreen
The Cerne Abbas giant in Dorset. Left image taken in August 2023, right taken August 2026. Composite: Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images


Both adaptation to and mitigation of the effects of a warming planet are urgently needed, said Dr Chloe Brimicombe, a climate scientist at the University of Oxford.
“This summer has been a compounding of dry weather,” said Brimicombe, “leading to droughts and hot weather and high temperatures leading to heatwaves with these conditions also leading to wildfires. It is a strong indication that we need better long-term planning. Climate change is not a future problem; it’s a challenge for right now.”
As the climate crisis supercharges “whiplash” wet-then-dry weather, the UK and Europe are seeing back-to-back heatwaves that encourage vegetation to grow but then dry it out, producing ideal fuel for fires.

Earlier this week, tourists were urged by a French official from Bordeaux’s surrounding region of Gironde not to visit until the “situation is under control”. 
Peter Sammonds, professor of geophysics and climate risks at UCL, said: “The human body struggles to cope in 33℃ weather, and for some it can be even lower.  
“Going forward, British tourists need to become aware of these risks, similar to how they would when travelling somewhere like Egypt or Cyprus. Tourists do not think about these things when going to France.” 
In 2024, France was the second-most visited country by British tourists, amassing 9.3 million visits, according to the Office for National Statistics. 
The wildfires have been influenced by El Niño, a Pacific weather pattern that increases global temperatures.  
But Bentley said: “El Niño will add extra warmth to the global climate, but it isn’t the main reason Europe is experiencing these extremes.”

That summer’s blazes had left two people dead in the northern region of Castilla y León and another man there fatally burned after the excavator he was using to try to dig a firebreak to protect his town was swallowed up by the flames. A street-sweeper in Madrid had collapsed and died from heatstroke while on shift in soaring temperatures that summer. The paramedics who tried to save him noted that his body temperature was 41.6C (107F).

“I want to make something very clear,” the prime minister told reporters in Extremadura that day in 2022. “Climate change kills: it kills people, as we’ve seen; it also kills our ecosystem, our biodiversity, and it also destroys the things we as a society hold dear – our houses, our businesses, our livestock.”

What is a frequent flyer levy? 
Currently, the Government charges Air Passenger Duty (APD) on every passenger aged over 16 who departs from a UK airport. The aircraft operator pays the fee, but the cost is usually passed on to passengers through their ticket price.

In 2021, the NEF and Possible climate charity proposed scrapping APD and replacing it with a new frequent flyer levy. 
Under the proposal, a passenger’s first leisure flight of the year would be tax-free, with each subsequent flight charged progressively more. Business flights would be taxed from the first trip. 
The idea, in short, is that a small number of wealthier, frequent flyers are responsible for a disproportionate share of flying-related emissions, so should pay more. In contrast, people who fly only once a year should pay less than they do now. 
The Government’s own climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), also proposed a similar system in 2019. 
However, their preferred model works differently. Rather than a flat rate that rises purely with the number of flights taken, it would charge per tonne of carbon emitted, meaning the cost also depends on the distance flown and the class of ticket bought.

articles.jina_text:
As homeowners look for ways to cut their energy use and reduce their reliance on gas, increasingly, heat pumps are becoming an attractive alternative to gas boilers. They produce fewer carbon emissions and, in the right property, can help to lower heating costs. Government support has made the upfront investment more manageable, too, with eligible households able to claim up to £7,500 towards installation, through the Boiler Upgrade Scheme.
But a heat pump is still a major home improvement, and the financial calculation goes beyond running costs alone. Homeowners may also wonder whether installing one will make their property more appealing to future buyers, improve its energy performance certificate (EPC) rating or even increase its eventual sale price.
The answer is not straightforward. A well-designed system in an efficiently insulated home could become a valuable selling point, but experts caution that buyers rarely pay a pound-for-pound premium for energy upgrades. Here, surveyors, property specialists and housing experts explain what homeowners should consider before investing.

How heat pumps work
Heat pumps work by extracting heat from the air or ground outside and using it to provide heating and hot water within a property. Unlike conventional boilers, which cycle on and off as temperatures rise and fall, heat pumps operate more steadily, maintaining a consistent indoor temperature. 





Although electricity costs more than gas per unit, a heat pump can typically generate around three units of heat for every unit of electricity it consumes. This means energy bills can be lower, particularly when combined with off-peak electricity tariffs or solar panels.
Heat pumps can cost between £8,000 and £15,000 to install but upfront installation costs have become more manageable, thanks to the government's Boiler Upgrade Scheme, which offers homeowners up to £7,500 in grants. The average price to replace a gas boiler is around £2,000 to £3,000. With incentives in place, many homeowners are now asking whether a heat pump is also a genuine investment when it’s time to sell their property.

ECB official warns climate crisis poses growing threat to ‘core financial stability’


Exclusive: As wildfires rage, Frank Elderson says more work needed to assess risk from collapse of ecosystem services




A senior policymaker at the European Central Bank has said the climate emergency and the breakdown of nature poses a dramatically growing risk to the global economy.
Frank Elderson, a member of the ECB’s executive board, said the eurozone lender of last resort was stepping up its monitoring of the financial risks linked to the destruction of “ecosystem services”, which are nature-related processes or assets that support human activity.

“These services are not stable but they are in rapid decline. That’s why we talk about the climate and nature crises,” he said. “So knowing that dependency, and knowing those exposures by the banks, we come to the conclusion that this is relevant.”
Across France and Spain, wildfires have raged amid record-breaking temperatures, torching land, businesses and homes, in an emergency that will carry a heavy economic cost beside the direct human toll.



In an interview with the Guardian before the current devastation across Europe, Elderson said it was clear the rising frequency of natural disasters linked to global heating pos a threat to financial stability.
He said more work needed to be done to assess the risk from the collapse of ecosystem services, as reliance on nature was more complicated to map than the impact of a single extreme weather event.
Ecosystem services are defined as any benefit that can be drawn from a natural structure or process – for example, water can be used as a raw material, an energy source through hydropower, or for transportation. It is also a habitat for marine life critical for food production, and a basis for recreational services.
“Nature-related risks can pose material economic and financial risks, including through their impacts on credit risk, growth, inflation and – over the long-term – potential financial instability,” Elderson said.
“I did interviews [previously] saying, you know, if you destroy nature, you destroy the core on which our economies depend. And that got people’s attention. This is not some kind of a flower-power, tree-hugging exercise. This is core economics. This is core financial stability, core price stability.”


As the supervisor responsible for Europe’s largest banks, the ECB has launched a programme of work to assess how the escalating damage to ecosystem services could expose the financial system to risk.
The central bank plans to publish analysis later this year investigating how “ecosystem degradation pathways” could translate into credit loss dynamics for the eurozone’s banks.

articles.jina_text:
India’s monsoon is in danger and hotter, drier conditions are forecast across much of the world as a stronger El Niño weather system is taking hold, weather experts have warned.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said the strengthening El Niño was “adding fuel to a planet already on fire” and pushing the world into “uncharted territory”.

The El Niño system will strengthen from August to October, which will bring higher temperatures globally, with increasing rainfall in some regions while others suffer drought, according to data and forecasts released by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Friday.
Marine heatwaves have already shocked scientists this year and are set to intensify: the WMO said temperatures were likely to exceed 2.9C above normal in several regions.



“The Pacific waters driving it have never been this warm this early in an El Niño, and temperatures are still increasing,” Guterres said. “[This year] risks shattering every seasonal record, and driving even more severe effects worldwide. We are in uncharted territory.”
The risk of a weakened monsoon, which brings the rain on which Indian farmers rely, was highlighted as the forecast gave an “enhancement in the probability for below-normal rainfall”, which would produce increased drought, floods and wildfire risk around the Indian Ocean basin. Drier conditions are also likely across parts of equatorial Africa to the west of the Horn of Africa, across the south and east of Australia, large parts of South America and in North America.
Higher than normal rainfall is expected in southern Europe, central Asia and the Horn of Africa and south-eastern South America.
Extreme weather has already caused havoc around the world this summer, with record-breaking heatwaves beginning in May in the UK, and wildfires across France and Spain that have destroyed villages and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.


View image in fullscreen
A destroyed house after wildfires in the village of Le Porge, Gironde, France. Photograph: Catalina Martin-Chico/The Guardian


Scientists have warned this year of the development of an El Niño, a weather system in the Pacific that frequently affects temperatures and rainfall around the world. Some El Niño years in the past have been relatively mild, but scientists have said that this year’s has been supercharged by the climate crisis.
Warmer waters – earlier in the year than usual and with water temperatures still increasing – have led to predictions of a “super El Niño” forming. The WMO does not use this term, but has said that the weather system developing is likely to be significantly stronger and more intense than usual. Friday’s forecasts were the organisation’s latest update, covering August to October.

articles.raw_rss: A Reform UK motion argues the council can improve the local environment without the official pledge.
articles.raw_meta: A Reform UK motion argues the council can improve the local environment without the official pledge.
articles.jina_text:
A local authority has voted to scrap a borough's climate emergency declaration, despite opposition from rival councillors and environmental campaigners.
South Tyneside's Reform UK councillors backed a motion at Thursday's full council meeting to rescind the 2019 pledge, arguing the authority could continue improving the local environment without maintaining the declaration.
The motion, brought by cabinet member for housing Steve Smith, said: "Core services, economic growth and the cost of living should take priority over climate targets that are not statutory requirements."
The motion was passed by 35 votes to 11.
Opposition councillors warned the move would weaken the Reform-led council's response to climate change and whether it would deliver any financial benefit, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
The original motion, launched by the Green Party, set out deadlines for the council to become carbon neutral, aligning strategic decisions, policies and strategies to this goal, as well as advocating for carbon reduction across the borough.
'False choice'
Smith's motion asked the council to "rescind" the pledge and request council officers to "review any policies, targets and spending commitments" introduced as a result of the declaration.





Advertisement












It also asked the council to "reaffirm its commitment to clean streets, parks, recycling, flood protection and other local environmental services that matter to residents" and to ensure future environmental initiatives are only pursued where they are "affordable, evidence-based and delivering clear benefits" for residents.
But councillor Rachael Taylor, Green group leader, said the motion "created a false choice between climate action and delivering good local services".
She said the council already "considers affordability, value for money and evidence before spending public money" and there was no evidence rescinding the declaration would save money or improve services.
Meanwhile councillor Kate Owens-Palmer, of the South Tyneside Alliance Group, said she was "perplexed" that the motion stated Reform wanted to rescind the climate emergency declaration, while at the same time, pledging to "do all the things that are going to protect nature and look after the climate".
The council meeting followed a demonstration from environmental campaigners outside South Shields Town Hall raising concerns about the motion.

‘It’s too fast, too big’: speed of climate crisis is devastating crops, say farmers


Drought and extreme heat are killing plants, driving up prices while also making some farms economically unviable




“It’s a constant battle,” says Tim Young. He and his family have been tracking the rainfall on their Norfolk farm since 1976, and the data shows the last six years have seen two-thirds the amount of rain compared with previous years. The lack of water has become the number one risk to Young’s business.
This summer has seen record-breaking climate induced heatwaves scorch much of Europe, which combined with droughts and “apocalyptic” wildfires has made farming virtually impossible. France has faced down fires that its president, Emmanuel Macron, called the worst since the second world war and on Wednesday half of England was declared officially in drought, with July expected to be the driest on record after winter floods, according to the Environment Agency. So how are farmers bearing up under the pressure?



“The vines are dying. The grass is yellow and now we can smell the smoke,” Uyen Do, an organic farmer in the Dordogne region of France says, almost in tears. “It’s already very difficult to survive economically and now with climate change it’s becoming a struggle that I’m not sure we’re capable of going through.”
Do took over the farm in 2018 and adopted organic farming practices in the hope to build resilience against the climate crisis. But with the climate changing much faster than most predicted, Do says her farm is just not able to adapt quickly enough. “It’s too fast. It’s too big,” she says.


View image in fullscreen
The grain store on Tim Young’s farm in Hockwold, Norfolk is holding far less than usual this year because of the drought. Photograph: Jason Bye/The Guardian

Last year, the Environment Agency paused his licence to take water from the nearby river owing to low river flows, which he says had catastrophic impacts on his farm. He keeps anxiously checking his phone to see what the latest update will bring.
“In July, we had just 0.2mm of rain,” he says. “We’re so reliant upon that message.”

The extreme heat and drought stoking huge wildfires in Spain and France were made far more likely by the climate crisis, a scientific analysis has found.

The finding is the latest to pin the blame for the continent’s sweltering and deadly summer firmly on the heating caused by the burning of oil, gas and coal.

This year’s wildfires in western Europe have been made worse by a wet winter and spring, which boosted the growth of vegetation, which then dried out and provided fuel for the fires – so-called whiplash conditions. Global heating is making winters wetter and summers drier and hotter in Europe.

We can see parts of the country are suffering from "vegetation stress" where the development and growth of plants, grass and crops can be severely affected.
Experts have said the combination of next-to-no rainfall and prolonged hot weather is likely to cause significant issues for the farming industry and have an impact on agriculture and food supplies.
Scientists also warn the UK is facing a growing risk of water shortages in the decades ahead, driven by human-caused climate change and increased demand.









A comparison of satellite imagery of the UK in May and July shows the stark differences in plant health. To assess this, we have used something called the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) - a measure of how green and healthy vegetation is.
The biggest changes are visible across Conwy, Flintshire, Denbighshire and Merseyside, where areas that were previously a patchwork of green fields and grassland are now covered by light brown tones, indicating extensive vegetation stress.









Elsewhere, the data highlights more localised hotspots of stress around Peterborough, Lincolnshire and parts of mid and east Devon, where fields also appear significantly browner than a year ago.









This is in stark contrast to upland Britain - including much of Scotland's highlands and the Welsh mountains - which has remained closer to normal or, in some places, appear slightly greener.
Vegetation turning brown, even on this scale, does not mean the plants have disappeared or died, as grass, shrubs and some trees can recover once rainfall returns, provided their root systems remain intact.
However, falling groundwater levels during prolonged dry periods can also remove an important backup water source for trees and other deep-rooted vegetation.
And perhaps counter-intuitively, prolonged dry weather can raise the risk of flash flooding when it eventually does rain. That is because parched, rock-hard ground may struggle to absorb water at first, so some rainwater may simply run off the surface instead.









Dr Jess Neumann, an associate professor at the University of Reading, said while it is not unusual to see some browning in the summer, the "large expanses of dry grass in parks, lawns and gardens" are particularly noticeable this year.
Neumann added that British plants are "not adapted to prolonged summer droughts and hot weather", unlike in places like the Mediterranean.
This summer's "flash" drought is also notable for how quickly it has developed, given in early spring river flows, soil moisture and reservoir levels were generally around or above normal following a very wet start to 2026.
The recent repeated heatwaves have sapped moisture from soils and vegetation via evaporation, which has in turn increased demand for water for farming, industry and household use.

Climate change made the extreme conditions behind the wildfires burning across France and Spain far more likely, new analysis has found.
The study, released by the World Weather Attribution group on Friday, found that human-caused warming made the hot, dry and windy conditions that fuelled the fires at least twice as likely in south-western France and at least 20 times as likely in central Spain. The scientists described both figures as conservative estimates.
Fires have burned across the two countries since early July, destroying thousands of homes and displacing more than 250,000. They have been described as some of the worst on record in both countries, with 140,000 hectares burned in Spain and 115,000 in France since the start of the year, an area larger than the Isle of Wight in each case. 





Some blazes grew so fierce they generated their own weather systems, making them very hard to contain, and further high temperatures are forecast in both countries in the coming days.
Researchers examined the seven-day period of most dangerous fire weather in the worst-hit areas, using a measure called the Daily Severity Rating, which combines heat, dryness, wind and landscape conditions to gauge how hard a fire would be to put out once it started. They compared this year's conditions with observations of past summers and with a simulated pre-industrial climate.

Dramatic pictures showed a blaze ripping across grassland in Hornchurch. A fire also destroyed a large area of land in Rainham.

The cause of both fires in the borough of Havering is under investigation.




It comes after around 120 firefighters battled two major grass fires in Romford, east London, on Wednesday.




The risk from blazes in capital, now officially in a drought, is “very high” currently, according to a Natural England fire severity index.








London Fire Brigade (LFB) had its busiest 24 hours of 2026 on Wednesday, tackling 63 grass fires across the capital as temperatures topped 30C (86F).




Control officers took more than 1,300 emergency calls and crews went to more than 500 incidents, the brigade said. 




Almost 1,000 calls about grass fires have been made in the past week.




Eight fire engines and around 60 firefighters tackled the grass fire near South End Road in Hornchurch on Thursday.




At the height of the fire, around six hectares was alight, the London Fire Brigade said. 




The LFB was first called to the fire at 1.18pm with the fire brought under control by 3.22pm.

The Brigade's Control Officers took the first of 11 calls at 3.35pm and the fire was under control by 5.12pm.




To battle both blazes, firefighters used backpack blowers, which work just like leaf blowers.




They allow firefighters to push flames back into already burnt areas.




This is a tactic that provides a faster, more efficient attack on wildfires.




Wildfire beaters were also being used. The beater is made of a long handle with a flat piece of rubber at the end.

The whole of Wales is now in drought, as the UK struggles with extreme heat, wildfires and dry conditions that experts warn may linger until the autumn.




The UK has endured its fourth heatwave of the summer, with temperatures topping 35C, as health authorities warned England is on track this year for the highest number of deaths caused by such hot spells since current figures began.








Natural Resources Wales (NRW) has extended its drought declaration – which was declared for North Wales and the Upper Severn last week – to cover the whole of the country, after very little rainfall and sustained high temperatures.




Wales has received just 8% of its long-term average rainfall for July, and the country is on course to have its driest July since records began 190 years ago, NRW said.




Half of England is officially in drought, despite a very wet winter, as an extremely dry July compounded a dry spring, and the successive heatwaves have put pressure on water resources.




Fire chiefs say that wildfires are becoming a “recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities” in the face of a changing climate, as data showed July has been the busiest month on record, with firefighters responding to 393 wildfires across England and Wales.











The number of wildfire incidents recorded this year already matches the total annual figures seen in 2021, 2023, and 2024 combined, although the number is below the same point in 2025 when long-lasting drought and heat caused severe fire risk.




Phil Garrigan, chairman of the National Fire Chiefs Council, said: “Wildfires are no longer isolated or seasonal events. They are becoming a recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities and emergency services.”

He said blazes could burn for days in remote locations, challenging terrain and extreme temperatures, as he called for sustained investment in specialist training, modern equipment and research and technology to improve prevention and response.

In the latest wildfire, properties including a holiday park were evacuated and roads closed as firefighters battled a large heathland blaze on the Suffolk coast, at Dunwich Heath.

Trump has long urged the UK to increase drilling and claimed that Burnham had pledged to "open up the North Sea" in their first phone call together.

Ferocious flames continue to rage in parts of France and Spain, with no sign of abating. We chart the destruction in graphics and pictures

By Damian Carrington, Lucy Swan, Ana Lucía González Paz, Harvey Symons




The hellish infernos that have torn through parts of France and Spain have caused deaths, the evacuation of 330,000 people from their homes, widespread destruction and clouds of toxic smoke. Records have already been smashed and with the fourth heatwave of the European summer setting in, there are few signs of the waves of wildfires ending.
France has already surpassed the worst previous year for the size of the area burned, with August, usually the hottest month, yet to come.


In Spain, the cumulative number of fires in 2026 has also set a new record for this time of year, and the cumulative burnt area remains just below the level reached by late July during a devastating fire season in 2022.

Why have the wildfires been so bad?
The extreme severity of the blazes is the result of “whiplash” wet-then-dry weather this year, supercharged by the climate crisis. Last winter and much of spring in western Europe was very wet, encouraging heavy growth of trees, shrubs and other vegetation.



However, by May the first of a series of heatwaves had hit Europe. All heatwaves are made more intense and more likely by the global heating caused by fossil fuel burning. The heatwave at the end of June was the most severe ever recorded in Europe and would have been impossible without the added heat from more than a century of carbon pollution.
Western Europe’s hottest June

The high temperatures meant the hot atmosphere strongly evaporated water from rivers and lakes and sucked plants and soil dry, with the conditions made 80 times more likely by global heating. As a result of the drought conditions, vegetation became tinder and the risk of wildfires soared, leading to a series of wildfires scientists have described as “firewaves”.



The situation has been worsened by the unprecedented development of enormous “fire clouds” – pyrocumulonimbus – in France. These form from the heat from huge fires and become a self-feeding firestorm, spitting lightning bolts and sparking further blazes.


View image in fullscreen
A pyrocumulonimbus, or ‘fire cloud’, in the Fontainebleau forest region, about 37 miles south of Paris, France. Photograph: Emma Da Silva/AP


View image in fullscreen
Firefighters use controlled burning to halt a wildfire near Cebreros, Ávila province, Spain.  Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP
The severity of the fires has been extremely challenging for the fire-fighting authorities, who in the past would have expected to extinguish the fires. One firefighter, Javier García, told Associated Press he had never faced anything like it in his two decades in the job.


“The evolution is alarming,” he said, adding that they were now prioritising evacuations and property protection because fast-moving walls of flames were too ferocious.

articles.jina_text:
England is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths this summer after the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) announced that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves.
The record was set in 2022 with 2,985 deaths, and August, traditionally the hottest month, is yet to arrive. The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said: “My thoughts are with all those who have lost loved ones as a result of the long and intense heatwaves.”

The UKHSA analysis estimated there were 753 deaths in the the heatwave from 24 to 27 May and a further 2,124 between 21 and 28 June. The total is almost double the figure for the whole summer in 2025.
The UKHSA estimate is based on recorded deaths. It calculates the excess mortality during the heatwaves when compared with mortality levels at similar times of the year that did not experience heatwaves. The figures are similar to an estimate published on 13 July that used a different method, based on data showing the link between heat and deaths in the past.



Heatwaves are made more intense and more likely by the fossil-fuel-driven climate crisis; the heatwave that affected western Europe at the end of June was the most severe and widespread ever. The heat in 2027 will be exacerbated by a looming super El Niño weather system and temperatures will continue to rise until carbon emissions are cut to net zero.
“The new figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people’s health,” said Dr Ross Thompson, principal environmental public health scientist at UKHSA. “As the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme. That’s why it’s vital that individuals, communities and systems are prepared to deal with higher temperatures, and to ensure those most vulnerable are protected.
Cooper said this summer’s heat was having “an increasingly serious impact on the health of thousands of people, and on the pressures facing our NHS too. My heartfelt thanks go to the NHS staff, care workers and emergency responders who have worked tirelessly through these exceptionally busy and challenging months to protect and care for people affected by the heat.”
Some ambulance services reported a record number of calls during the heatwaves.


During the June heatwave in England a new high temperature for the month, of 38C, was recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk, while the 31.5C recorded at Kew Gardens in May was a new record for that month.
Dr Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, of Imperial College London and co-author of the 13 July study, said: “The UKHSA’s analysis provides clear, tragic confirmation of the significant health impact these heatwaves had across England and Wales. Firefighters are tackling a huge blaze near a nuclear power plant in Suffolk as authorities declared a “major incident” and residents have been evacuated.
At least 90 firefighters are tackling the “large-scale, wind- driven forestry fire” which broke out on Dunwich Heath shortly after 5:30pm on Wednesday, the Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service said.
Residents in several coastal properties and caravans have been evacuated as crews issued an urgent plea for people to stay away from the area.





There is no current risk to Sizewell B – a nuclear power station which provides electricity to 2.5 million households – due to the distance of the fire, but firefighters warn it is a “live and dynamic situation”.
It comes after forecasters warned any wildfires that break out in the South of England this week could become “exceptionally severe” due to a prolonged spell of hot and dry weather across the country.
The UK has experienced record-breaking temperatures this summer, with four heatwaves and a severe dry spell that has left the landscape parched.


At the height of the third heatwave in mid-July, firefighters were battling 19 significant wildfires simultaneously in England and Wales.

Weatherwatch: rainclouds are travelling farther in warmer world


Climate crisis affects not only the amount of rain that falls but where, with implications for land use and water security




Have you ever wondered how far a raindrop has travelled before it lands on you? It may have journeyed thousands of kilometres from the ocean, sea or lake it evaporated from – and now research shows raindrops are travelling even farther than they used to.
Warmer air can hold more water vapour, and that is changing not only how much rain we receive but also where it falls. Travis Aerenson, of the University of Wyoming, and his colleagues modelled atmospheric moisture movements in the US over more than three decades. Their research showed that in the southwestern and southern plains, moisture in the atmosphere travels 30 to 50 miles (50 to 80km) farther than it did 35 years ago, staying aloft for an extra two to four hours before falling as rain.

Their findings, published in Geophysical Research Letters, also show that more evaporation is occurring from ocean surfaces and less from land surfaces. The change in atmospheric moisture pathways affects where and when precipitation occurs, with implications for land use. The researchers also note that the trend for moisture to travel farther will result in the water security of more countries and states falling increasingly outside their borders, requiring greater collaboration between neighbours.

Half of England officially in ‘exceptionally serious’ drought


Environment Agency names seven regions affected by unusually hot and dry weather and shortage of water




Half of England is officially in drought, with July set to be the driest on record after winter floods, the Environment Agency has said.
The “flash drought” developed quickly because of unusually low rainfall and high temperatures.

The seven areas officially in drought are East Anglia, Hertfordshire and the whole of London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex (covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and south Gloucestershire).
Helen Wakeham, the director of water at the Environment Agency and chair of the National Drought Group, said: “The hot and dry weather means we are currently using water faster than nature can replenish it.


“A second consecutive summer drought is an exceptionally serious situation and one that will have long-lasting impacts on our environment, wildlife and the economy.
“We want everyone to stay safe and hydrated during the hot weather but every drop we can save is a drop more for nature and agriculture.”
Wednesday’s announcement means England has experienced drought in three of the past five years: 2022, 2025 and 2026.
July has had only 7% of the expected rainfall, falling to 1% across southern England, with no substantial rainfall on the way. Some parts of Devon have not experienced any rain for 50 consecutive days.

articles.jina_text:
Since mid-July wildfires have torn through France, Spain, and Portugal forcing more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes.
Officials in the Spanish capital Madrid have said the fires are the worst the region have ever experienced.
French President Emmanuel Macron, visiting the fire-ravaged area in the Gironde region, called the "completely unprecedented" wildfire the "toughest since World War Two".


The fires have broken out amid a sweltering summer of heatwaves across Europe. Both France and Spain are now seeing another sharp rise in temperatures, with peaks of 41-42C expected in France.
Wildfires in the regions outside Madrid have burned about 606 sq miles (1570 sq km) since 1 July, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (Effis). That is an area more than twice as large as the city itself. 


















In France, the worst affected area has been the Gironde, around the city of Bordeaux, where more than 200,000 people were forced from their homes. 
From 22 July the blaze spread rapidly, tearing through forests and fields in France's famous wine region, and burning more than 162 sq miles (420 sq km) in less than four days - an area roughly four times the size of Paris.
At its peak, the wildfire came as close as nine miles (15km) from the south of Bordeaux, although the city was never under serious threat.
The fires have also came close to a number of sensitive military and industrial sites in the area, including facilities that work on French ballistic missiles, rocket motors, and the processing of hazardous chemicals.


The fires became so extreme they created their own giant fire thunderstorm. 
A rare weather event, storms like these are formed when heat from the wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly, carrying smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere.
As the air rises, it cools, and the water vapour condenses into a cloud. If the fire is powerful enough and the atmosphere is unstable, that cloud can grow into a cumulonimbus - the same type of cloud associated with thunderstorms.










If these clouds then become large enough, they can produce their own lightning, which can then start new fires. They can also occasionally bring hail and rain.


These extreme and unpredictable conditions make the fires all the more difficult to stop.
To combat them, French firefighters have been using planes loaded with fire retardant, as well as planes like the Canadair, which can scoop 6,000 litres of water from lakes or the sea in 12 seconds and drop it directly on the fires.
On dangerous days, loaded aircraft patrol high-risk areas before any fires have been reported, so they can drop within minutes of a sighting. Planes often fly in a continuous shuttle while retardant is laid along the edges of the fire and ground crews attack the flames directly.

Caribbean bears brunt of £43bn climate-fuelled damage to developing islands


Findings can inform conversations about global climate reparations and financing for mitigations, researchers say




Caribbean nations suffered $53.2bn (£40bn) of damage from climate-fuelled disasters between 2000 and 2024, research into the cost of the climate crisis to developing small islands has found.
The figure is more than 90% of the total $57bn in economic damage caused by floods, storms and drought across 39 developing island nations in the Caribbean, the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, according to a study by development thinktank ODI Global.

ODI Global also estimates the climate crisis caused more than 190 deaths a year over the 25-year period studied.
The research is important for conversations about global climate reparations, the report’s author, Emily Wilkinson, said.


The Caribbean has been pursuing climate justice after bearing the brunt of the crisis, which is primarily caused by high carbon emitters outside the region.
Several Caribbean countries provided evidence to the international court of justice, the world’s top UN court, in a case that ended last year with a landmark advisory opinion that could mean states are ordered to pay compensation if they fail to tackle fossil fuels and prevent harm to the climate system.
Wilkinson said: “There have always been hurricanes, heavy rainfall, drought and temperature extremes, historically, but it’s really important to be able to say what percentage of that kind of strength or intensity is actually due to increasing global temperatures.
“Climate scientists do these attribution studies and they’re really important for when we start to think about responsibilities for the impacts of climate change, compensation and climate reparation.
“[They] tell you what kind of proportion of the intensity of the event is due to climate change. We’ve taken it a step further by doing an additional calculation, which is a fraction of attributable risk, to work out what percentage of the damage that’s been reported can be attributed to climate change.”

The closure of the strait of Hormuz has created conditions for an extreme global biodiversity threat, with scientists warning that thousands of stranded ships could spread invasive marine species across the world’s oceans once they begin sailing again.
More than 1,500 commercial vessels have been stuck in the Gulf since the strategic waterway closed on 28 February after the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran. An international team of marine biologists said that with the stranded ships remaining motionless, their hulls were becoming encrusted with marine life – from microbes and algae to barnacles and other invertebrates – that could hitchhike to ports around the world when trade resumed.

Prof Mario Tamburri, of the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science and the study’s lead author, said: “If you had to design the worst-case scenario, I don’t know if you could have done it differently. It is a perfect storm.”
The research describes the situation as a potential marine “bio-invasion super-spreader event”, arguing that no previous shipping disruption has involved so many vessels remaining idle for so long.
According to the study, ships normally only remain at anchor in a harbour for one to three days, limiting the growth of organisms on their submerged surfaces. But many vessels trapped in the Gulf have remained stationary for months, allowing dense marine communities to establish themselves.
If thousands of vessels leave carrying barnacles, algae, mussels and other organisms, they could introduce invasive species that outcompete with native wildlife, spread disease and permanently alter marine ecosystems.
“When you move organisms around, they can reduce biodiversity in the regions they invade, cause local extinction of organisms that they displace,” Tamburri said.
Invasive species can also devastate fisheries, clog the cooling systems of power plants and cost billions of dollars a year to manage, he added.

Organic eggs have worse impact on climate than eggs from caged chickens


Adopting organic free-range model in UK could lead to greenhouse emissions equivalent to 2,316,000 tonnes of CO2, study suggests




Organic eggs are twice as bad for the climate as eggs from chickens living in cages, research suggests.
According to the study, switching the UK’s entire egg production to an organic free-range model would lead to greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to 2,316,000 tonnes of CO2 (tCO2e), while production through a fully caged system would emit 1,184,000 tCO2e.

This is because organic free-range models need more chickens for the same number of eggs produced, as birds living in cages tend to be more efficient.
Organic free-range production also scored worst in its potential for water eutrophication, acidification and land use. Chicken mortality was also highest in organic free range farming, the researchers said.


However, the study used data from 2009-2010, which the researchers acknowledged as a limitation as it did not capture more recent developments in egg production. The research also did not take into account other environmental impacts such as pesticides or biodiversity.
Laying hens are the largest group of animals kept in cages across the world, and global egg consumption is going up, making their treatment an important welfare consideration, said Dr Harriet Bartlett, one of the authors of the study.
“I’d say perhaps it’s also a little bit of a blind spot when we talk about sustainability,” she added. “Meat and dairy get a bit more attention, talking about environmental sustainability, whereas [egg production] hasn’t been as researched.”
Bartlett is the senior research associate at Oxford University’s Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment, and has previously studied factory farming methods.
The latest study, published in Royal Society Open Science, involved Bartlett and colleagues examining data from UK poultry farms to calculate environmental impacts such as greenhouse gas emissions, land use and types of pollution. They also looked at welfare indicators such as mortality and the number of hens needed to produce a given number of eggs.


“Then we did some some modelling to work out these environmental and welfare outcomes,” she said.
“We found an important trade-off,” Bartlett added. “It’s that, the types of farms that are generally regarded as being better for animal welfare, like organic and free-range, can actually require more birds to produce the same amount of eggs because they’re less less efficient and they can have higher environmental impacts.”

The sky outside is hazy orange, and my five-year-old son is screaming bloody murder. “Sorry, buddy, we have to stay inside,” I say. “It’s not safe to breathe out there.” I had told him we’d be going to the beach today. Something inside me tears a little as I wonder how many promises he’ll see similarly broken in the coming years.

Some of them already had to tell their kids that their Fourth of July festivities were canceled because of the lethal heatwave that caused numerous mass casualty events earlier this month.

According to scientists, these extreme weather events are not “natural” disasters. A team of researchers already published a study finding that the Fourth of July heat wave would have been “virtually impossible” but for the climate crisis. A salt marsh in the Outer Hebrides provides an “almost unbroken record” of sea level changes over the last 2,500 years, scientists have said.




Researchers studying the marsh at Gress on the Isle of Lewis had originally been searching for deposits left by the Storegga tsunami, a massive wave triggered by an underwater landslide off Norway around 8,200 years ago.








Instead they were surprised to uncover 2,500 years of geological history preserved less than two metres beneath the surface, recording how sea levels have changed since around 500 BC.




They said the findings provide one of the most detailed records yet of how Scotland’s coastlines have responded to shifting climates and changes in the elevation of land since the end of the last Ice Age.




Dr Uisdean Nicholson, a sedimentary geologist from Heriot-Watt University’s School of Energy, Geoscience, Infrastructure and Society, said: “Salt marshes are incredibly sensitive to changes in sea level, so they preserve a detailed history of how coastlines evolve over time.




“And this one at Gress turned out to hold an almost unbroken record of the past 2,500 years.




“It’s amazing to get a snapshot of what the environment was like so far back in time, when the Persian empire was at its greatest extent and the Roman Republic was just getting started.”


The team analysed sediment cores taken from the marsh (Sue Dawson/PA)

Professor Sue Dawson, an expert on geohazards from Geography at the University of Dundee, said: “This painstaking work gives us an understanding of the way the rising and falling sea level has influenced the vegetation and the algae that grow and live in our coastal environments, which helps to unlock the sea level story”.

ByJaroslav Lukiv and Yang Tian







27 July 2026
Updated 4 hours ago




Spain and France are bracing for new heatwaves with temperatures expected to soar past 40C in some regions.
Spain's national weather service says the severe weather is forecast to last until "at least" Sunday, and warns of "extreme" fire risks as firefighters continue to battle the some of the worst blazes in the country's history.
France's south-west regions Gironde and Landes are under "yellow alert" for a heatwave expected to peak on Wednesday, further hampering efforts to contain "very unpredictable" blazes in Gironde.
The mayor of Bordeaux has said he is preparing for "all eventualities", as one of the wildfires burning in France is 15km (nine miles) from the south-western city.
"We are preparing to accommodate a large number of people should further evacuations be ordered," said Thomas Cazenave. 
Some 220,000 people have been evacuated in France and more than 100,000 in Spain, where fires are burning "uncontrolled" west of Madrid.
President Emmanuel Macron, visiting the fire-ravaged area in the Gironde region, said the country was facing a "completely unprecedented wildfire" - the "toughest since World War Two".
Macron said a smaller fire in the Landes region had been contained, but the fight continued in neighbouring Gironde. 
While firefighters had made progress on Monday, Macron warned that "temperatures are set to rise again, the wind is still present, and therefore we must remain humble".
Earlier, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had said the fire "has a life of its own".
Jerome Steffe, the mayor of Cestas, a town south of Bordeaux, told the BBC this "will be the fire of the century".
He described how 17,000 residents were evacuated from his town during the night when the fire swelled two days ago. So far, he said, the region has seen 42,000 hectares (103,000 acres) of land burned and 240 houses destroyed.
"In my city the situation is really catastrophic," he added.
And although the fire is no longer moving as quickly, he said his teams have "won only a small battle" and emphasised that the risk remains from flying embers or a sudden change in wind direction.
"We put all our energy into creating protective firebreaks," he explained, but admitted "we are all scared in front of this situation."
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned the country "is going through an unprecedented fire season", with 116,085 hectares (286,852 acres) burned and 13,566 fire starts recorded since January.
The minister revealed in a post on X that nine out of 10 fires "are human-caused and most arise from carelessness: a cigarette butt, a barbecue, work carried out without precaution".
But he also said that not all these fires are accidents and some are deliberately set, adding that since 6 July, 162 arrests have taken place.

Editorial





At a time when the quickening pace of global heating has never been clearer, climate policies are being deprioritised





A new and ominous word has entered the vocabulary of firefighters struggling to cope with the vast wildfire sweeping through south-west France. A pyrocumulonimbus is a fire-generated thunderstorm that can whip up winds in unpredictable ways, making the containment of a blaze and assessment of its likely course far more difficult. A known phenomenon in North America and Australia, firefighters believe France is suffering its first in the Bordeaux region, as the country endures the consequences of the third major heatwave of the summer and prepares for a fourth.
The dire statistics of the ongoing fires in France and Spain tell a story of deepening devastation and human misery. A far greater expanse of French land has already been burnt this year, compared with the 30,000 hectares during the whole of 2025, while 220,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the Gironde. In Spain, the environment ministry has calculated that over 170,000 hectares have been affected, compared with 29,000 last year. Over 100,000 people have been forced to flee.



View image in fullscreen

Aid agencies have called on prime minister Andy Burnham to address drivers of inequality, injustice and poverty following the decision to reallocate international aid to help fight the climate crisis towards funding a cap on UK bus fares. 
The heads of 98 organisations, including Oxfam GB, WaterAid and ActionAid UK, have warned that countries already trapped in unfair debt cycles could be left with few choices but to borrow more to address the climate crisis. They highlighted that the crisis is not of their making.
“Politicians must stop pitting the needs of the British public against the needs of people in the majority World by raiding the already diminished UK aid budget to fund domestic spending,” the joint statement said. “Both face many of the same underlying challenges.”





The prime minister announced last week that he would change international climate donations into repayable loans to reduce the fare cap from £3 a journey to £2 next year. Around £400 million is expected to go towards the initiative by replacing international climate finance grants with loans, allowing the government to borrow more without violating its borrowing rules. 
Charities have said that the world’s most vulnerable people will be put at risk by the decision.

In the BBC’s new apocalypse drama, The Rapture, the UK is engulfed in a terrifying heatwave. I watched a preview of the programme in May, while preparing to interview the lead actor Ruth Madeley. I thought at the time: “This will be much more frightening when it chimes with the real life weather, bad luck for them that it’s not coming out for a couple of months.” But, by the time of meeting Madeley the following month, we were already in the middle of a heatwave that would lead to the highest ever recorded June temperature in the UK. The whole encounter made the show feel even more prophetic. She was in a central London hotel, air-conditioned inside, but all the door handles and surrounding street furniture – benches segmented by metal arm rests, to make life just that little bit harder for homeless people – had got way too hot. It was like playing The Floor is Lava, except instead of “floor”, “everything”. It surely can’t hit the screens at a more apposite time than this, I thought, failing to predict that by late July we’d be in heatwave number three, and France would be on fire.






The Rapture review – this apocalyptic drama couldn’t be here at a better time







Read more

The Daily Mail’s reviewer was upset that Christianity was portrayed “as a bastion of anti-science nutjobs and fundamentalists” in the show, wondering rhetorically whether the BBC would ever create such a drama about a “Muslim imam”. Peculiar thing to get upset about, I thought, since the religion is really more of a symptom of, or even a garnish to, the central atmosphere of engulfing heat. It’s like complaining that cats get a bad rap in the 1974 film The Towering Inferno (yes, there is a cat in it).
TV puts a particular pressure on itself to describe the world it lands in, even when a show is developed at least a couple of years before. Often, the safe way to play it with surrounding factors – weather, politics, fashion – is to keep things so general that they could be any time this century. PM urged to uphold climate pledges made as mayor and ban new North Sea oil drilling


Experts who helped Burnham draw up Manchester carbon neutral pledge say backtracking would send wrong message amid wildfires and heatwaves




Leading climate scientists who created Greater Manchester’s carbon neutral by 2038 commitment are urging Andy Burnham to unequivocally reject new drilling in the North Sea.
In a letter to the prime minister they said he, as mayor of Greater Manchester, had unveiled one of the UK’s most ambitious local climate programmes that tackled housing, green growth and public transport.

Reports over the weekend continued to suggest Burnham was set to give the green light to controversial new drilling in the North Sea by approving the Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfields, which were given approval under the Conservatives but put on hold by legal action. The ruling in court said a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact was required to take into account the effect on the climate of burning any fossil fuels extracted.


Prof Kevin Anderson and scientists from the Tyndall Centre at the School of Engineering at the University of Manchester, who wrote the open letter to the prime minister, said it was “with considerable concern” that they had read reports suggesting his government intended to approve the further development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields.
To do so would send a signal around the world that the UK was backtracking on its international climate commitments, they said.







Burnham risks Labour backlash if he reverses ban on new oil and gas drilling

Read more
If the reports were accurate that he intended to give the go ahead to drilling at Jackdaw and Rosebank, the scientists wrote, “they represent a profound departure from the principles you promoted as Mayor of Greater Manchester”.
Labour made a manifesto promise that no new oil and gas licences would be issued, but Jackdaw and Rosebank were already in the system at the time of the last general election. A consultation on Jackdaw will finish on 8 August.
With extreme heat and wildfires across the UK and Europe this summer, the academics said the evidence showed global emissions must be cut by 8% every year if the world was to meet the upper limit of a maximum of 2C of heating in the Paris climate agreement.


Anderson and his colleagues urged Burnham to adhere to commitments he made when announcing the Greater Manchester carbon neutral by 2038 policy.
